clue.text: Till unlimited crop etc, save water

indicators.note: each of the four words loses its limits, its first and last letters, leaving only the insides

explanation.surface: A farmer told to plough while sparing the water supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlimited' applies to every word that follows, not just 'crop', so each of the four is stripped of its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To till ground is to break up the soil, which is what a rotary cultivator does when it churns a field.

clue.text: Conscious of beginning with conception, then aftermath

indicators.note: the abbreviation for with comes at the start, before the other pieces

parts.note: a conception is an idea
the wake of something is its aftermath, what follows in its track

explanation.surface: Someone becomes aware of a pregnancy and then of what it brings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' sits on the charade: W, the abbreviation for 'with', comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Fully alert and aware of everything around, the hyphenated phrase works as an adjective for conscious.

clue.text: Offensive posters prompted by promenade cycling

indicators.note: the letters of the word for a promenade go round, the first one moving to the end

parts.note: a promenade is a stroll, a leisurely walk

explanation.surface: Rude flyers inspired by people riding bikes along a seafront walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves the S of STROLL from the front to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Internet users who post deliberately provocative messages to upset others are known by this name.

clue.text: Part of our Channel diplomacy's ending again, amid shifting blame

indicators.note: the final letter of diplomacy's goes in among the rearranged letters of blame
the letters of blame shift about into a new order
the ending of diplomacy's is its last letter

parts.note: again asks for the same final letter of diplomacy's a second time

explanation.surface: A cross-Channel diplomatic row ends with the blame being passed around once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'again' repeats the Y from 'diplomacy's ending', so a second Y follows the anagram of BLAME with the first inside; the blogger found 'amid' loose for that.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyme Bay is a large inlet of the English Channel on the Devon and Dorset coast of south-west England.

clue.text: Pest from the West: part of picture, one about Boatman

indicators.note: only the first letter of picture is taken, a small part of the word
the word for one goes around the setter's pronoun

parts.note: an means one, as in an apple
Boatman is the setter, who refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: Pest from the West is a Buster Keaton short, and the setter is reaching for one frame of that film.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter's own name, so it stands for I; AN goes about it, after the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is a nuisance or annoyance is often called a pain, as in a pain in the neck.

clue.text: Railcar put in motion — not at all like The General

definitions.text: not at all like The General

indicators.note: the letters are set moving and come to rest in a new order

explanation.surface: The General is Keaton's railway film, and a railcar set moving recalls its locomotive chase.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on 'general' as the opposite of the answer, in the sense of specific rather than general.
explanation.definitionFit: Specific or individual is the opposite of general, so it is not at all like the general case.

clue.text: See 23
See 15
See 2
Sequence from The Cameraman rewound for club

indicators.note: like a film reel wound back, the letters are read in the other direction
a run of consecutive letters is taken from inside the words

explanation.surface: A film editor rewinds a scene from Keaton's The Cameraman to use for a club.
explanation.walkthrough: The run E, C, A, M spans 'thE CAMeraman'; 'rewound' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy club with a spiked or flanged head, used as a weapon in medieval times, is a mace.

clue.text: Appear lately to be untruthful in report?

parts.note: to be untruthful is to lie
to report is to state

explanation.surface: Someone seems to have given a false account in an official report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lately' means 'the late', the dead: a dead dignitary appears in public before burial.
explanation.definitionFit: A deceased dignitary displayed publicly in a coffin before the funeral makes an appearance as the late person.

clue.text: The Invader's leader lost, missing the Italian beers

indicators.note: the Italian article is absent from what remains
the word loses its first letter, its leader

parts.note: invaders who loot are pillagers; the possessive gives the final S
il is the Italian for the

explanation.surface: Keaton's The Invader loses its star, and Italian drinkers go short of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: PILLAGERS without its leading P gives ILLAGERS; taking out IL leaves the beers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a light, fizzy beer, so beers of that kind are lagers.

clue.text: Submit reward for audience initiative

parts.note: to submit an entry is to enter it

indicators.note: for listeners the word is heard rather than read, so it sounds alike

parts.note: a prize is a reward

explanation.surface: An entrant hands in work hoping to win a prize from the judges.
explanation.walkthrough: PRIZE said out loud sounds like PRISE, the spelling the answer uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing enterprise means showing initiative, the readiness to start new projects.

clue.text: Next hopeless job candidate, parts of bio absent, not hired at last

indicators.note: a hopeless job candidate is all over the place, so the letters are jumbled
the letters of bio are missing from the jumble
the final letter of hired is not in the jumble either

parts.note: the separate letters of bio are taken out, scattered rather than in a run

indicators.note: only the final letter of hired is meant

explanation.surface: The next applicant is hopeless: their CV is missing bits and they were never hired.
explanation.walkthrough: From JOB CANDIDATE remove B, I, O and D (the last of 'hired'); 'hopeless' mixes the rest, JCANDATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something next to another thing is neighbouring or alongside it, which is what adjacent means.

clue.text: Not a fan of Sherlock Jr — or my aim, it is not true!

indicators.note: the letters are not true to their order, so they must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Keaton's Sherlock Jr meets a hostile critic, with 'not true' as the heckle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sherlock Jr' is Keaton's film, but 'Jr' belongs to the letters being mixed, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Holmes's arch-enemy in the BBC series Sherlock is the criminal mastermind called by this first name and surname.

clue.text: Is livid to watch The Saphead

parts.note: to watch is to see
taken as written
read as Sap head, the head of sap is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone furious at being made to sit through Keaton's The Saphead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saphead' is read as 'Sap head', the head of 'Sap', which is S.
explanation.definitionFit: To be livid is to be furiously angry, and someone boiling with rage is said to fume or simmer.

clue.text: Venerable in middle age

indicators.note: only the central letters of venerable are kept

explanation.surface: An old person who has reached middle age.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a long period of history marked by some feature, the same span of time as an age.

clue.text: Material United Artists may argue lacks global appeal, missing their premieres

indicators.note: the premiere of each word is its first appearance, its opening letter

parts.words: Artists may argue lacks global appeal, missing

explanation.surface: A studio claims a film lacks worldwide appeal because nobody attended the premieres.
explanation.walkthrough: United Artists was the studio that released several Keaton films; 'United' is only part of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Amalgam is a blended substance, most familiar as the mercury alloy used in dental fillings.

clue.text: Admits every wrongdoing involving heartless outlaw

indicators.note: the word for every and the word for wrongdoing together wrap around the other piece

parts.note: every means all
sin is wrongdoing

indicators.note: the heart of outlaw is removed, keeping only its outside letters

explanation.surface: A confession to every crime in which a gang member, minus his heart, played a part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts the outside letters of 'outlaw' inside the charade of the two other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To let someone or something enter is to admit them, so the phrasal verb means admits.

clue.text: Old readers embracing comic art at The Playhouse?

indicators.note: the archaic pronoun holds the rearranged letters inside it

parts.note: thee is an old word for you, as in you readers

indicators.note: art is made comic, jumbled up into a funny new order

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned readers enjoy comic art at Keaton's film The Playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Thee is singular, so 'readers' is a loose fit for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A playhouse is a building where plays are staged, the same as a venue for drama.

clue.text: A cook embraces pepper crust method

indicators.note: the cooking word holds the outside letters inside it

parts.note: to poach is to cook gently in liquid

indicators.note: the crust is the outside of pepper, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A chef wraps a pepper crust around a dish as a cooking technique.
explanation.definitionFit: An approach is a way of tackling a problem, so it means a method.

clue.text: Steamboat Bill once passed after ending up with King Edward's crown on board

indicators.note: the law word comes after the letter from up
the ending of up is its last letter
the crowning letters go aboard, inside the other letters

parts.note: a bill once it has been passed by Parliament becomes an act

indicators.note: the crown is the top, so the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: Keaton's Steamboat Bill Jr, a boat with royal passengers aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending up' gives P, then ACT, with K and E from 'King Edward's crown' inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A packet boat was a steamer carrying mail, passengers and goods on a regular route.

clue.text: Just a rotation in a crop

indicators.note: a letter inside the cereal word turns round to a new place

parts.note: barley is a cereal crop

explanation.surface: A farmer explains that a field is simply part of a rotation of crops.
explanation.walkthrough: The E in BARLEY moves one place left, before the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Barely means only just, as in barely enough to get by.

clue.text: Funny rebuke about person who did good work a hundred years ago, a comic genius

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the saint
rebuke is made funny, scrambled into a new order

parts.note: a saint did good works; ST is the abbreviation
a ton is a hundred

explanation.surface: A comedian being scolded about a good deed done a century ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'years ago' only sets the scene: Keaton's silent films came out a hundred years ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Keaton was the great stone-faced silent-film comedian, celebrated as one of the finest of all screen clowns.

clue.text: Balanced matches, playing soccer where clubs cut grass back

indicators.note: the letters of soccer play about into a new order
one letter is cut from soccer

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: the grass word reads backwards

parts.note: sward is grassy turf

explanation.surface: Football clubs drawing their games while the groundsman mows the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: SOCCER minus one C gives SOCER, which 'playing' turns into SCORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A football match that ends level with both sides scoring goals is called a score draw in British football pools.

clue.text: What you'll see in a diary, regularly ending in darkness

definitions.text: What you'll see in a diary

indicators.note: every other letter of a diary is taken, at regular intervals
the last letter of darkness is used

explanation.surface: A diarist records something written at the end of each dark night.
explanation.definitionFit: A diary is laid out by date, so it is filled with entries for each twenty-four hours.

clue.text: Sell hard One Week

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
a means one

explanation.surface: One Week is a Keaton short, here sold hard as a marketing push.
explanation.definitionFit: To hawk goods is to peddle them, offering them for sale from place to place.

clue.text: Try for goal, not starting to laugh

indicators.note: the word loses its first letter, it does not start

parts.note: to try for goal is to shoot

explanation.surface: A footballer misses a shot and the crowd fails to start laughing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoot is a loud burst of laughter, as in hoots of mirth.

clue.text: Try South Africa, as briefly suggested

indicators.note: the short form of the country, spoken letter by letter, suggests the word

explanation.surface: A rugby try for South Africa, as the summary hinted.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters S and A, said out loud, give 'ess ay'.
explanation.definitionFit: An essay is an attempt; to essay something is to try it.

clue.text: Articles drawn from Cairo and Tehran read back in persuasive speech

indicators.note: what is left of the city names is read from the end to the start
the articles are pulled out of the two city names

parts.note: a and an are the indefinite articles in English

explanation.surface: Speeches drawing on news articles from two Middle Eastern capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: A comes out of Cairo and AN out of Tehran, leaving CIRO TEHR to be turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhetoric is the art of persuasive or impressive language, often used of grand speech.
